jurisdiction: Boulder County (every Boulder County ballot, including all of the City of Boulder)
official_title: Shall Boulder County taxes be increased $30,000,000 annually (in tax collection year 2027), and by such additional amounts raised annually thereafter, by a mill levy imposed at a rate of 2.579 mills (equating to approximately $115 per year on a $725,000 home based on current rates of assessment) for the purpose of addressing the shortage and high cost of child care and preschool programs for Boulder County families with young children, including: lowering the high cost of child care and preschool for Boulder County families; increasing the compensation of child care and preschool teachers and staff to retain and attract high-quality educators; and addressing the shortage of care by expanding capacity for more children and reducing waitlists; and shall the revenues and earnings on the investment of the proceeds of such tax constitute a voter-approved revenue change under Article X Section 20 of the Colorado Constitution and an exception to the limitations set forth in Section 29-1-301 of the Colorado Revised Statutes, all as more particularly set forth in Board of County Commissioners' Resolution No. 2026-048?
plain_summary: A new county property tax of 2.579 mills, about $115 a year on a $725,000 home, raising about $30 million a year for child care and preschool. The money would lower costs for families, add spots for infants and toddlers, and raise pay for child care workers. It starts with 2027 tax bills and has no end date.
yes_means: Boulder County property taxes rise 2.579 mills starting with 2027 bills, with no end date, raising about $30 million a year for child care and preschool.
no_means: No new county child care tax; your county property tax does not change for this purpose.
current_law: There is no dedicated countywide child care tax today; the county's resolution says a local source would add stability as state and federal funding becomes less certain. The resolution says care costs more than $23,000 per child per year, licensed infant and toddler care is scarce (a shortfall of about 1,723 infant and 1,357 toddler slots), and child care staff turnover runs 20% to 30% a year.
fiscal_impact: TABOR notice: up to $30,000,000 in the first full year, growing as property values grow. The county estimates 2026 spending of $329,783,240 (up 18% since 2022) and $339,433,199 in the first full year without the increase. Cost: about $16 per $100,000 of actual home value per year (about $115 on a $725,000 home). Administration may not exceed 10% of annual revenue, and the money may not replace existing funding.
confusing_wording_note: Tax questions in Colorado must open with 'Shall ... taxes be increased,' so that wording is standard, not a warning sign. 'And by such additional amounts raised annually thereafter' means the rate stays at 2.579 mills but the dollars grow as home values grow, so the $115 figure is today's estimate, not a cap. The ballot doesn't say how long the tax lasts; the county resolution behind it says it continues 'in perpetuity' unless voters repeal it.

supporters_case.text: The comment filed for 1A in the TABOR notice says Boulder County has licensed spaces for only about 25% of infants and 50% of toddlers who need care, that care can cost $20,000 to $23,000 per child a year ('more than a year of in-state tuition at CU Boulder'), and that the cost is 'less than $10 per month' on a $725,000 home. It says the plan was built by local parents, providers and employers and the money stays local. The Daily Camera, the League of Women Voters of Boulder County and the county commissioners support it.

opponents_case.text: No comments against 1A were filed for the TABOR notice by the deadline. The Boulder County Republican Party urges no, calling it 'a permanent property-tax hike with a built-in TABOR carve-out' and saying the spending categories are broad and the tax never sunsets. PLAN-Boulder County took no position, saying it sees the need but residents are already being asked for 'more and more taxes.'

official_title: Shall the membership of the Boulder County Board of Commissioners be increased from a three member board to a five member board?
plain_summary: Grows the Boulder County Board of Commissioners from three members to five. If it passes, new districts are drawn in 2027, the new seats are elected in November 2028, and five commissioners take office in January 2029. Question 201 decides how they'd be elected.
yes_means: Starting in January 2029, Boulder County is governed by five commissioners instead of three, elected the way Question 201 decides.
no_means: The board stays at three commissioners, and Question 201 has no effect.
current_law: Three commissioners run the county, as they have since 1861. Each lives in one of three residency districts, but all three are elected by voters of the whole county. They oversee a county budget of more than $745 million for over 330,000 residents (Daily Camera). Commissioner salaries are set by the state at $158,000 a year.
fiscal_impact: No official cost estimate was found. The Daily Camera, which supports the measure, estimates two more commissioners' salaries, benefits and related costs could reach about $500,000 a year, roughly 0.07% of the county budget.
confusing_wording_note: 200 and 201 are a pair. 200 asks whether to expand; 201 asks how the expanded board would be elected. Vote on both: your choice on 201 only counts if 200 passes, and answering 201 does not count as a yes on 200. Nothing changes this year; the new seats are first elected in 2028. The 'Commissioner District 3' race on this same ballot is a separate, current seat.

supporters_case.text: PLAN-Boulder County says three at-large commissioners now decide for more than 330,000 residents in a county whose population has more than doubled since the 1970s, and five would give 'fairer, more balanced representation' from cities to farms to mountains. The Daily Camera, the League of Women Voters of Boulder County and the Boulder County Republican Party also support it; the GOP says it spreads representation 'beyond Boulder's political center.'

opponents_case.text: No organized opposition was found in the sources collected, and the county commissioners took no position. The main concern raised is cost: the Daily Camera, while supporting it, notes about $500,000 a year at a time the county is trimming its budget, and says the change 'would not automatically make the commissioners more responsive.'

official_title: If the membership of the Boulder County Board of Commissioners is increased from a three member board to a five member board, by what method shall the Boulder County Board of Commissioners be elected? (1) Five commissioners resident in districts to be elected only by voters resident in the district; or (2) Three commissioners resident in districts to be elected only by voters resident in the district; plus two commissioners resident in any district to be elected by voters of the whole county.
plain_summary: Only matters if Question 200 passes. You choose how a five-member county commission would be elected. Option 1: five districts, and you vote only for the commissioner from your district. Option 2: three districts elected by district voters, plus two commissioners elected by the whole county. The petition that put 200 on the ballot was required by state law to offer these two choices.
yes_means: This is not a yes/no question. Picking option 1 means all five commissioners would be elected only by voters in their own district.
no_means: Picking option 2 means three commissioners would be elected by district voters and two by the whole county. If Question 200 fails, neither option takes effect.
current_law: Today all three commissioners are elected countywide, each from a residency district. If 200 passes, the board must set up a redistricting commission in 2027 to draw the districts.
pass_threshold: whichever option gets more votes; takes effect only if Question 200 passes
confusing_wording_note: Your ballot shows two ovals labeled with the option text, not 'yes' and 'no'. In the fields above, 'yes' describes option 1 and 'no' describes option 2. Below, the supporters' case is the case for option 1 (five districts) and the opponents' case is the case for option 2 (three districts plus two at-large). Pick one even if you vote no on 200, in case 200 passes.

supporters_case.text: For option 1 (five districts): the Daily Camera says two at-large seats 'would likely lead to two additional voices from either Boulder or Longmont,' the county's population centers. The Boulder County Republican Party also picks option 1, saying it keeps 'Boulder's population center from dominating every race.'

opponents_case.text: For option 2 (three districts plus two at-large): the League of Women Voters of Boulder County supports this mix 'until Boulder County has the option to elect county commissioners using a method which promotes proportional representation.' City candidates who answered Boulder Reporting Lab's survey split between the two options.

official_title: Residential vacancy excise tax (TABOR) Shall the City of Boulder taxes be increased $6,000,000 annually (which amount represents estimated revenues in 2028, the first full fiscal year of collection), and by such amounts raised annually thereafter, by imposing a $4,000 tax on vacant homes that are occupied for 183 days or less per year, with such amount never falling below $4,000 but increasing annually in accordance with the Denver-Aurora-Lakewood consumer price index up to, but never exceeding $7,000, with the revenue from such tax to be used for the purpose of supporting City services, including: police and fire protection; parks and recreation; transportation and maintenance; and other general services important to the quality of life in the City; and shall the revenues from such taxes and any related earnings be collected, retained, and spent as a voter-approved revenue change without limitation and an exception to the revenue and spending limits of Article X, Section 20 of the Colorado Constitution?
plain_summary: A $4,000-a-year city tax on Boulder homes lived in 183 days a year or less, rising with inflation to no more than $7,000. The first full year of collection is 2028. The money goes to general city services like police, fire and parks, not specifically to housing.
yes_means: Owners of Boulder homes occupied 183 days a year or less pay a $4,000 yearly city tax (rising with inflation, capped at $7,000) for general city services.
no_means: No vacancy tax; owners pay no extra city tax for leaving a home empty most of the year.
current_law: Boulder has no vacancy tax. A city estimate cited by Boulder Reporting Lab puts the number of vacant homes at 500 to 1,000. City Council sent the measure to the ballot 7-1. A citizen petition for a $7,000 vacancy tax was started earlier in 2026 and dropped.
fiscal_impact: Ballot and TABOR notice: $6,000,000 in 2028, the first full year. Other estimates are lower: Boulder Reporting Lab reported a city estimate of about $4 million a year, and the Daily Camera says $1 million to $2 million. City TABOR figures: 2026 spending estimated at $425,612,000 (up 47% since 2022); $570,000,000 projected for 2028 without the tax. No estimate of the cost to run and enforce the tax was found.
confusing_wording_note: The title says 'vacancy,' but the money is not set aside for housing; it goes to general city services. The $6 million on the ballot is a TABOR estimate, and other city and press estimates are much lower. The ballot does not say how 'occupied' is defined or how the city would check; the one comment against in the TABOR notice raised exactly that, and the Daily Camera says the city might rely on water-use data. 'Excise tax' here just means a flat fee per vacant home, not a percentage.

supporters_case.text: No comments for 2J were filed for the TABOR notice. Council's stated goal is to encourage owners to rent or sell vacant homes and add to the housing supply (Boulder Reporting Lab). The county commissioners support it. Most city candidates who answered Boulder Reporting Lab's survey, including all four responding mayoral candidates, said they would vote yes. The League of Women Voters of Boulder County is neutral.

opponents_case.text: The one TABOR comment against says the tax could hurt some homeowners and lacks detail on property types, how residency is defined and how it would be enforced, with privacy concerns. The Daily Camera says vacancy is hard to prove and the revenue too small to justify staff and possible legal fights. PLAN-Boulder County says it would be costly and complicated to run. The Boulder County Republican Party calls it a 'punitive' tax on how often you use your own home.

official_title: Recreation and Safety Bond (TABOR) Shall City of Boulder debt be increased up to $400,000,000, with a maximum repayment cost up to $650,000,000, and shall city taxes be increased up to $32,500,000 annually for the purpose of financing the construction, renovation, or replacement of community recreation, safety infrastructure, and other capital projects, such as: (I) the South Boulder Recreation Center, including a lap pool; (II) the North Boulder Recreation Center, including aquatics amenities and improvements needed to co-locate West Age Well Senior Center; (III) fire stations (to sustain emergency and wildfire response capabilities); (IV) a new Public Safety Building for police and 911 services; (V) Penfield Tate II Municipal Building; and (VI) the Municipal Service Center (to support infrastructure services, such as snow removal, utility maintenance, and city street operations); In order to support recreation, safety, and critical infrastructure needs for community members of all ages; Through the issuance and payment of general obligation debt, with such debt containing such terms, not inconsistent herewith, as the City Council may determine; and in connection therewith, Shall ad valorem property taxes be levied without limitation as to the rate, but not more than the amounts listed above, to generate an amount sufficient in each year to pay the principal of, premium, if any, and interest on such debt or any refunding debt (or to create a reserve for such payment); and Shall the proceeds of such debt and reserves and the revenues from such taxes and any investment income earned from such proceeds and revenues be collected and spent without limitation or condition as a voter-approved revenue change and an exception to the limits that would otherwise apply under article x, section 20 of the Colorado constitution or any other law?
plain_summary: Lets the city borrow up to $400 million (up to $650 million with interest) to fix or replace aging buildings: the South and North Boulder rec centers, fire stations, a new police and 911 building, and city service buildings. A new property tax repays it, about $400 a year per $1 million of property value if the city borrows it all.
yes_means: The city may borrow up to $400 million for recreation, safety and other city buildings, and property taxes rise (about $400 a year per $1 million of property value at full borrowing) until the debt is repaid.
no_means: No bond and no new property tax. The city says it would patch its most urgent buildings with existing money and has no plan to pay for a new South Boulder Rec Center or police building.
current_law: The city maintains more than 75 buildings, and more than a dozen are near the end of their useful life; the city puts the unfunded backlog at about $400 million. Its existing 0.3% sales tax for capital projects (CCRS) is already committed to planned projects through 2031. The city has made three rounds of budget cuts since 2025. It owes $191,075,000 on existing bonds. Council voted unanimously to send 2K to the ballot.
fiscal_impact: TABOR notice: principal up to $400,000,000; maximum annual repayment $32,500,000; total repayment up to $650,000,000. City spending without the increase: $552,600,998 in the first full year. The city estimates about 6.352 mills (about $400 a year per $1 million of property) at full borrowing over 20 years, and says it would likely borrow in stages, so the full increase is unlikely for a couple of years. The city's project estimates add up to about $444 million, more than the $400 million cap; it plans to sell some buildings to cover the gap.
confusing_wording_note: The project list says 'such as,' so it is a list of examples, not a promise. Boulder Reporting Lab reports the ordinance lets the money go to 'other capital projects as approved by City Council' and that 'the list is not binding.' 'Without limitation as to the rate' is standard bond wording: the tax rate can move to cover the payments, but the dollars are capped at $32.5 million a year and $650 million in total. The tax is temporary even though the title says 'taxes be increased'; it ends when the bonds are paid. The $170 million police building figure may change: the city manager has since raised buying or leasing an existing building instead (Daily Camera). Question 2M, which raises the city's debt limit, is described by Boulder Reporting Lab as a companion measure, but the city's materials do not say whether 2K depends on it.

supporters_case.text: The one TABOR comment for 2K says these building needs 'will still have to be addressed even if this measure fails,' that bonds spread costs to the current and future residents who benefit, and that each project would still get public comment and Council review. The city says the police building's systems are failing, with leaks and mold concerns, and South Boulder Rec is cramped, inaccessible and deteriorating. The League of Women Voters of Boulder County supports it.

opponents_case.text: No comments against were filed for the TABOR notice. The Daily Camera urges no for now, calling the plan 'undercooked' and noting Broomfield is building a police headquarters for $82 million versus $170 million here; it asks for a citizen oversight committee and a better proposal next year. PLAN-Boulder County says it supports fixing the buildings but not '$650 million at something that is so ill-defined,' citing cost overruns on other city projects. The Boulder County Republican Party says each project should be asked for separately.

official_title: Bargaining Rights Union Firefighters in City Charter Shall the city amend its charter by the addition of a new Sec. 73, "Collective Bargaining for Firefighters," as described in Ordinance 8761 which provides a charter guaranteed right for full-time fire department employees to bargain collectively over matters related to safety, wages, benefits, and all other terms and conditions employment, except those certain terms that are reserved to rights of management as defined in the proposed charter amendment, with impasse to be resolved through non-binding factfinding followed, if necessary, by a vote of the qualified electors of the City?
plain_summary: Puts Boulder firefighters' right to bargain as a group over pay, benefits and working conditions into the city charter. If talks deadlock, a fact-finder makes non-binding recommendations, and then Boulder voters can decide. Firefighters already bargain under a contract and city ordinance; this moves those rights into the charter.
yes_means: Firefighters' right to bargain collectively, and the deadlock process (fact-finding, then a public vote), become part of the city charter, which only voters can change.
no_means: Nothing changes now: firefighters keep bargaining under their existing contract and city ordinance, not the charter.
current_law: The city says collective bargaining rights for firefighters 'currently exist in contract, and the right to take disagreements to impasse is currently in a city ordinance.'
fiscal_impact: No official cost estimate was published; this is not a tax measure.
confusing_wording_note: This does not create a new union; Boulder firefighters already bargain through a contract. The county Republican guide describes 2L as letting firefighters 'unionize,' which does not match the city's description. 'Resolved ... by a vote of the qualified electors' means an unresolved contract dispute could end up on a future Boulder ballot for voters to settle. 'Non-binding factfinding' means the fact-finder's recommendation is advice, not an order.

supporters_case.text: The Daily Camera urges yes: 'our firefighters deserve this basic right,' and says it matters for wildfire preparedness. Every city candidate who answered Boulder Reporting Lab's survey said they support it, and Council referred it unanimously after negotiating it with the union.

opponents_case.text: The Boulder County Republican Party urges no: it says it supports firefighters but that putting bargaining in the charter is permanent, will 'drive up costs' and leaves future councils 'far less flexibility' on budgets and pay. The League of Women Voters of Boulder County is neutral.

official_title: Debt Limit City Charter Language Change Shall Section 97 of the Boulder Home Rule Charter be amended pursuant to Ordinance 8762 to modify the City's debt limitation to be not more than three percent of the actual value of the taxable property within the City?
plain_summary: Changes the city's debt limit from a share of property's 'assessed' (taxable) value to 3% of its 'actual' market value. The city says this allows more borrowing than today. 2M doesn't borrow money or raise taxes by itself.
yes_means: The city's debt limit becomes 3% of the market value of taxable property in Boulder, which the city says allows more borrowing than today.
no_means: The current charter debt limit, based on assessed value, stays in place.
current_law: Charter Section 97 limits city debt based on the assessed value of taxable property. The city's materials do not state the current percentage or dollar limit; the Boulder County Republican guide says it is 6% of assessed value.
fiscal_impact: No direct cost. The city has not published, in the materials collected, how much the borrowing limit would rise.
confusing_wording_note: 'Three percent' sounds lower or stricter than today. It is not: market value is many times larger than assessed value (the Republican guide estimates about 15 times), so 3% of market value is a much bigger number. The city's own summary says the change allows 'more debt than is currently permitted.' Boulder Reporting Lab calls 2M a companion to the 2K bond, and the Daily Camera ties the two votes together, but the city does not say whether 2K depends on 2M.

supporters_case.text: The city says basing the limit on actual value 'is consistent with how most municipalities and the state calculate debt limitation.' The League of Women Voters of Boulder County supports it, citing 'efficient fiscal administration' and updating charters 'when necessary for good fiscal administration.'

opponents_case.text: The Daily Camera says: 'If you voted no on 2K, vote no on 2M.' The Boulder County Republican Party calls it 'a permanent expansion of Boulder's borrowing power' and says if the city wants more debt for a project, 'it can bring that project to voters.'
